title: Erewhon
subtitle: or, Over the Range
pitch: A satirical utopia where people smashed their machines centuries ago, because a philosopher warned that machines were evolving towards consciousness faster than humans.

chapters.g: The narrator translates an Erewhonian treatise: consciousness appeared once from lifeless matter, so why not again, in machines.
The writer argues machines are already evolving, served by humans who feed and breed them, and that their pace far outstrips ours.
Objections and replies, and the conclusion that drove the Erewhonians to destroy most of their machines.

ideas: Machines might evolve as living things did.
Humans could become servants of the machines they depend on.
Machine progress is far faster than biological evolution.
A society might choose to give up technology out of fear.

args.a: Machines could develop a kind of consciousness through evolution.
args.c: Butler wrote partly as satire, poking at Darwinian ideas and Victorian faith in progress.

args.a: Destroying machines is a rational response to the risk.
args.c: The Erewhonians are shown as odd, and the novel mocks their extremes as much as it supports them.

questions: Is Butler joking, serious, or both?
Are we already servants of our machines?
What would a modern Book of the Machines say?

quiz.q: What did the Erewhonians do with their machines?
quiz.w: Out of fear of machine evolution.

quiz.q: What earlier piece did Butler write on the same theme?
quiz.w: An 1863 letter, also in this library.
